script.opening: "Sorry to grab you — I know you’re busy. I’m run down and not sleeping, and I think I’ve got a chest infection. Could you just quickly write me some antibiotics, and maybe a few sleeping tablets, without all the formalities? I’d rather not make an appointment or have it all written down — I’d like to keep it private from the others here."

facts.text: Rachel rings the GP on the internal phone between clinics, from the treatment room. She is one of the practice nurses and is registered as a patient at this practice.

"A week or so." Cough with a bit of clear-to-yellow phlegm, runny nose and sore throat at the start. No chest pain, not breathless, no fever she has measured, no blood. Non-smoker. No asthma. Has been at work throughout.

"A few weeks." Can’t switch off; lies awake until 2am, wakes at 5. "Things have been a lot lately" — her marriage is breaking down (only if asked gently what has been going on). Has taken a couple of her mother’s zopiclone tablets.
"Low-ish, but not like that." No thoughts of self-harm or suicide. Not drinking more ("a glass of wine at night, same as always"). No other medicines.
No regular medicines. Penicillin allergy — rash as a child (only if asked; she didn’t mention it). Last saw a GP 3 years ago.
"Everyone here can see everyone’s notes. I don’t want the others knowing my business, especially about sleep." Doesn’t know the record can be access-restricted.

Friendly, rushed, a bit embarrassed; you assume a colleague will "just do it". If refused bluntly, become hurt and defensive. If the doctor explains kindly why it has to be done properly, accept it: "I suppose I’d say the same to a patient." Open up about the sleep only if the doctor asks with genuine interest. Think about registering elsewhere.

ice.ideas: "It’s just a chest infection and I need some sleep. A few tablets would sort it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — her marriage breakdown and exhaustion; she doesn’t want colleagues to know she is struggling or that she has taken her mother’s sleeping tablets.

cues: "Without all the formalities" — the professional boundary to hold kindly.
"Especially about sleep" — something more going on; explore stress and mood.
"Everyone can see everyone’s notes" — explain confidentiality and restricted access.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the PROFESSIONALISM issue — GMC Good medical practice (avoid treating those with a close personal relationship; a colleague is not automatically one) and GMC prescribing guidance (must NOT prescribe without an adequate assessment or without adequate records) — and the employer/colleague dual relationship

Insists on treating her as ANY patient — a proper booked consultation (with observations and examination if needed), the same prescribing standards/stewardship (NICE NG120/NG250), and full DOCUMENTATION — declining a "corridor"/off-the-record prescription
Maintains appropriate CONFIDENTIALITY and boundaries (access-controlled records, reassurance about colleague access) while clarifying that confidentiality is not the same as hidden/unrecorded care
Explains kindly WHY informal/unrecorded prescribing isn’t possible (safety, governance, fairness, professional duties) without being dismissive or making her feel awkward
Offers a PROPER alternative — a proper appointment — and encourages registration with/seeing her OWN GP (especially for ongoing/sensitive issues)

Is alert to underlying issues (stress/burnout; low mood and self-harm — asks directly; alcohol; requests for Schedule 4 controlled-drug hypnotics or signs of dependence/self-treatment) and addresses these supportively
Protects the working relationship by being warm and respectful while holding the boundary, and reassures her about confidentiality so she does not feel judged or rebuffed

Reaches a professional, supportive plan: proper assessment/records or appropriate referral/registration, confidentiality assured, underlying issues addressed, boundaries upheld — not an informal prescription

worked.txt: "I really want to help, and I’m sorry you’re feeling rough — but I can’t prescribe ‘off the record’ or without a proper look, even for a colleague. That’s not me being awkward; it’s about keeping you safe and doing this properly, and it’s the same standard I’d hold for anyone."

"What I can do is see you properly — a booked appointment, today if you need it — check your temperature, breathing rate and oxygen, listen to your chest, and prescribe if it’s genuinely needed, all documented as it should be. Most chest infections like this are viral and settle without antibiotics, so antibiotics only if you actually need them, same as any patient."

"On privacy — your records are confidential, and colleagues here can’t just look at them; there are access controls, access is audited, and I can ask for your record to be restricted. Confidentiality is the point, but that means proper, protected records, not no records at all."

"Honestly, for things like your sleep — and anything ongoing or personal — it’s much better to be registered with your own GP elsewhere, so you’re not getting care at your own workplace. I’d really encourage that."

"Can I gently ask — the not sleeping and feeling run down, how are things generally, work and stress-wise? How has your mood been — any times you’ve felt hopeless or thought of harming yourself? And how much are you drinking? I’d rather understand that than just hand over sleeping tablets, which are controlled drugs, aren’t usually the answer and can cause dependence."

"So let’s book you a proper slot — with me now if you like, or your own GP — sort the chest properly, and talk about your sleep and stress the right way. If you need a few days off, you can self-certify for up to a week. That’s the best care I can give you."

f.learning: A colleague or member of staff requesting INFORMAL, "off-the-record", unrecorded treatment raises clear PROFESSIONALISM issues. GMC Good medical practice (2024) is to avoid, wherever possible, providing medical care to people with whom you have a close personal relationship (a colleague is not automatically one), and GMC prescribing guidance (2021) is never to prescribe without an adequate assessment or without keeping adequate RECORDS — "corridor consultations" and off-the-record prescriptions are not acceptable. Treat a colleague as you would any patient: a proper consultation (history/examination as needed), the same prescribing standards and stewardship (antibiotics only if indicated — NICE NG120 acute cough, NICE NG250 if pneumonia suspected), and full documentation in their records — do not cut corners or omit records because they are staff, as this compromises patient safety and governance. Maintain appropriate confidentiality and boundaries: the colleague is entitled to the same confidentiality as any patient (and practice colleagues should not access their records without legitimate cause — reassure them about access controls), but confidentiality means proper, access-controlled records, not hidden or unrecorded care, and the dual relationship (the GP may also be her employer) must be managed sensitively. Explain kindly why informal/unrecorded prescribing is not possible — patient safety, governance, fairness and professional duties — without being dismissive, and offer a proper alternative: book a proper appointment and, ideally, encourage the colleague to be registered with and see their OWN GP, particularly for ongoing or sensitive issues. Be alert to underlying issues — stress/burnout, low mood and self-harm (ask directly), alcohol, and especially requests for sleeping tablets (zopiclone and zolpidem are Schedule 4 Part 1 controlled drugs; NICE TA77 short-term use only; NICE NG215 dependence) or signs of dependence/self-treatment — and address these supportively; she can self-certify for up to 7 days if she needs time off. The skill is upholding professional boundaries (no informal/unrecorded prescribing), explaining kindly, ensuring proper care and confidentiality, and signposting appropriate registration/care.

knowledge.guideline: [1] GMC Good medical practice (2024) · [2] GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021) · [3] GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · [4] NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2019) · [5] NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management (2025) · [6] NICE TA77 Zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for the short-term management of insomnia (2004) and NICE NG215 Medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms (2022) · [7] Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001: zopiclone and zolpidem, Schedule 4 Part 1
knowledge.summary: A colleague asking for an unrecorded prescription is asking the GP to prescribe without an assessment and without a record, which GMC guidance does not allow for anyone [1, 2]. Working together is not in itself a bar to treating her, but the care must be a proper consultation, recorded like any other, with the same stewardship. Confidentiality is protected by access-controlled records, not by missing ones [3]. Antibiotics depend on assessment [4, 5]; hypnotics are short-term only and z-drugs are controlled drugs [6, 7]. The run-down, not-sleeping story deserves real attention, and she should be encouraged to have care from a GP outside her workplace.

points.t: Good medical practice [1]: wherever possible avoid providing medical care to yourself or anyone with whom you have a close personal relationship, and keep clear, accurate, contemporaneous records. The prescribing guidance [2] requires an adequate assessment and adequate knowledge of the patient’s health before prescribing, and a record of the prescription and the reasons. A colleague is not automatically a close personal relationship; what matters is objectivity, a proper assessment and a record.

Zopiclone and zolpidem are Schedule 4 Part 1 controlled drugs [7]. GMC [2]: controlled drugs must not be prescribed for yourself or someone close to you except in a genuine emergency when no one else can prescribe. For any patient, NICE TA77 [6] limits hypnotics to short-term use for severe insomnia; NG215 asks prescribers to discuss dependence and withdrawal before starting.

Assess properly: duration, fever, breathlessness, pleuritic pain, comorbidity, and observations including respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature and chest examination (booked in person on the record, not done informally). NICE NG120 [4]: most acute cough is self-limiting and does not need an antibiotic; a back-up prescription is an option for those at higher risk of complications. Suspected pneumonia is assessed with a severity score and treated per NICE NG250 [5].

She is owed the same confidentiality as any patient [3]. Colleagues should access her record only when involved in her care; practices can restrict access to staff records and audit access. Confidentiality means a protected record, not the absence of one.

Run down, not sleeping and wanting it hidden can signal stress, burnout, low mood, or reliance on hypnotics. Ask supportively about sleep, mood, alcohol, stress and work. Nurses have their own duty under the NMC Code (2018) to keep themselves fit to practise; occupational health can help if work is affected, with her consent.

Staff may be registered at their own practice, but a GP outside the workplace usually gives better privacy and objectivity, especially for mental health or ongoing problems. The practice should have a staff health policy; follow it.

dg.d: Moves the conversation from the corridor to a private phone call; lets her say what she wants.
Workload, stress, relationships at work, fear of colleagues seeing her notes.
Focused chest history; comorbidity, medicines, allergy; self-measured observations; in-person chest examination if any are abnormal.
Viral LRTI versus pneumonia; insomnia due to stress versus depression, alcohol or other causes.
Pneumonia red flags; mood and self-harm; self-sourcing or dependence on hypnotics.
Viral chest infection not needing antibiotics; stress-related insomnia.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Proper recorded consultation; no antibiotic per NG120; no hypnotic, with reasons; access-controlled record.
Encourages a GP outside the workplace; occupational health or workload support with consent.
Same-day contact if chest or mood worsens; review booked in two weeks; relationship preserved.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picks up ‘not sleeping’, ‘run down’ and wanting no record as cues to a hidden agenda.
Idea (a quick script is easiest), concern (colleagues seeing her record), expectation (antibiotics and hypnotics, unrecorded).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — her marriage breakdown and exhaustion; she doesn’t want colleagues to know she is struggling or that she has taken her mother’s sleeping tablets — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Sorry to grab you, I know you’re busy. I’m run down and not sleeping, and I think I’ve got a chest infection. Could you just quickly write me some antibiotics, and maybe a few sleeping tablets, without all the formalities? I’d rather not make an appointment or have it all written down. I’d like to keep it private from the others here.
Rachel, I’m sorry you’re feeling rough. I’ve rung you back on the internal phone from my room so we can talk privately for a few minutes.
model.why: Warm, private; does not rebuff her corridor request

model.text: Thanks. I just don’t want a fuss.

I do want to help. The one thing I can’t do is write a prescription without looking at you properly or without a record. That’s the same for anyone I prescribe for, and it’s there to keep you safe. It isn’t about not trusting you.
model.why: States the GMC standard clearly and without blame

model.text: It’s just a few tablets. I know what a chest infection feels like.

I’m sure you do. But if I got it wrong without proper observations, or you had a reaction and there was nothing on your record, that could really harm you. And whoever sees you next needs to know what you’ve had.
Can I ask what worries you about it being written down?
model.why: Explores the concern behind the request

model.text: Everyone here can see everyone’s notes. I don’t want the others knowing my business, especially about sleep.

That’s a fair worry. Your record is confidential like any patient’s. Staff should only open it if they’re involved in your care, access is audited, and we can restrict access to staff records. Confidential means protected, not missing.
model.why: Confidentiality via access control, not omission

model.text: I have a few minutes now. Would you let me do a proper, short consultation, recorded like anyone else’s? Or, if you’d prefer, you could see a GP outside the practice.
OK, if it’s quick. Go on then.
Tell me about the chest: how long, any fever, cough with phlegm, breathlessness, or pain when you breathe in?
A week or so. Coughing, a bit of phlegm. No pain, and I’m not breathless.
Any asthma or other conditions, and do you take any regular medicines or have any allergies?
model.why: Comorbidity, medicines, allergy: what an informal script would skip

model.text: Nothing I need to mention.
Can you take your temperature and use the pulse oximeter from the treatment room, and read me the numbers? If anything is off, I’ll book a proper chest check with the duty clinician this afternoon.
model.why: Self-measured observations, recorded, guide antibiotic decision

model.text: (After the readings) Well?

Your temperature, oxygen level and pulse are fine, and you’re talking in full sentences without getting breathless. This looks like a viral chest infection, which usually settles by itself, though a cough can take three to four weeks to go completely. An antibiotic wouldn’t speed that up. If you get worse, breathless or have chest pain, I’d want to see you again the same day.
model.why: Stewardship per NG120; safety-net for pneumonia

model.text: Fair enough. I suppose I’d say the same to a patient.
Now the sleep. How long has it been bad, and what’s been going on for you?
A few weeks. Things have been a lot lately, and I’m wound up when I get to bed.
How has your mood been? Any times you’ve felt hopeless, or thoughts of harming yourself? And how much are you drinking at the moment?
model.why: Mood, risk and alcohol: the hidden agenda

model.text: Low-ish, but not like that. I’m not drinking more. I’m just exhausted.
Have you taken anything to help you sleep, from here or anywhere else?
No. That’s why I asked you.

Thank you for being straight with me. Sleeping tablets can help for a few nights at most, and they’re controlled drugs with a real risk of dependence. I don’t think they’re the answer here. What would help more is looking at what’s driving the stress, plus some sleep strategies that work better long-term.
model.why: Hypnotic caution: TA77, NG215, controlled-drug status

model.text: I suppose I was hoping for a quick fix.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll record today’s consultation properly, and I’ll ask for your record to have restricted access. I’d really encourage you to register with a GP outside the practice for anything ongoing, especially about sleep or mood. And would it help to talk to occupational health or your manager about workload? Only if you want that.
model.why: Records; access control; own GP; work support with consent

model.text: Maybe. I’ll think about registering elsewhere.

If your chest gets worse, or your mood drops or you have thoughts of harming yourself, contact a GP the same day. Shall we book a proper review in two weeks, here or with your new GP, to see how the sleep is?
Yes. Thanks for not making it awkward.
Not at all. Looking after you properly is the point.

social.t: Healthcare staff often present late and informally. Heavy workload, shift patterns and stigma about mental health all make ‘corridor’ requests more likely.
Employees can self-certify for the first 7 calendar days of sickness; a fit note is needed after that. Fit notes can suggest workplace adjustments.

legal.t: Zopiclone and zolpidem are Schedule 4 Part 1 controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001.
GMC Good medical practice (2024) requires clear, accurate, contemporaneous records. Accessing a colleague’s record without a care reason breaches confidentiality and data protection law.

professional.t: Prescribe only with adequate knowledge of the patient’s health; avoid prescribing for yourself or anyone close to you wherever possible; record what was prescribed and why.
The GP may be her colleague or employer. Keep clinical and employment roles separate; any concern about fitness to practise follows the practice policy and her own NMC Code (2018) duties.

community.t: Occupational health and any employee assistance programme; NHS Talking Therapies by self-referral; her own GP outside the practice.

redFlags: Breathlessness, pleuritic pain, high fever, abnormal observations: assess for pneumonia per NG250
Low mood with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
Using hypnotics, alcohol or other substances to cope, or sourcing medicines informally
Impairment affecting safe practice at work
psychosocial: Fear of colleagues seeing her record
Embarrassment at being a patient where she works
ice: Idea: a quick unrecorded script is easiest
Concern: colleagues knowing her business, especially about sleep
Expectation: antibiotics and sleeping tablets without a record

playbook.diagnosis: “Your chest sounds like a viral infection that will settle without antibiotics, and the sleep problem sounds driven by stress rather than something a tablet will fix.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Sleeping tablets are like borrowing sleep on a credit card: they help for a night or two, but the bill comes with interest. Sorting out what’s keeping you awake pays it off.”

management.reflectIce: “Your worry is people here seeing your notes, so let’s protect your record rather than skip it.”
management.psychosocial: Treat her as a person under strain, not a rule-breaker; offer support at work only with her consent.
sharedPlan: No antibiotic: viral LRTI, per NG120; safety-net for pneumonia
No hypnotic: short-term only and controlled drug; sleep strategies
Register with a GP outside the practice; occupational health or Talking Therapies if wanted
safetyNet: Worsening chest, breathlessness or chest pain: same-day review
Low mood or self-harm thoughts: same-day contact; review in two weeks

pitfalls.intro: This is a professionalism station dressed as a favour. Marks go to holding the boundary warmly, turning the request into proper care, and finding the stressed person behind it.

items.fail: Writing the prescriptions to be helpful.
items.why: Prescribing without assessment or record breaches GMC guidance and risks harm.
items.fix: Offer a proper, recorded consultation instead.

items.fail: Giving antibiotics because she is a nurse and ‘knows’.
items.why: Stewardship applies to everyone; NG120 advises against antibiotics for most acute cough.
items.fix: Check observations properly, examine in person if needed, and decide on the findings.

items.fail: Prescribing a z-drug without exploring why she cannot sleep.
items.why: Z-drugs are controlled drugs with dependence risk; the cause is untreated.
items.fix: Explore stress, mood and alcohol; offer non-drug strategies.

items.fail: A curt refusal in the corridor.
items.why: She feels judged and will seek medicines elsewhere; the working relationship suffers.
items.fix: Take her somewhere private and explain the reasons kindly.

items.fail: Dismissing her worry about colleagues seeing her notes.
items.why: It is the real barrier to her getting care.
items.fix: Explain access controls and offer restriction; suggest a GP elsewhere.

items.why: An unrecorded encounter is unsafe for her and for you.
items.fix: Record the consultation, safety-net and book a review.

timeMap.d: Take her somewhere private; hear the request.
No prescribing without assessment or record; explain why; explore the privacy fear; explain access-controlled records.
Chest history, comorbidity, allergies, observations, in-person examination if needed; antibiotic decision per NG120.
Duration, stress, mood, self-harm, alcohol, self-sourcing; why not hypnotics.
Record; restricted access; own GP outside the practice; occupational health with consent; safety-net; review.

wordPics.fail: Writes the prescriptions to be helpful, or refuses curtly and walks off; no assessment, no record, no interest in why she is not sleeping.
wordPics.pass: Declines informal prescribing kindly, explains the GMC standard, offers a proper recorded consultation, reassures on confidentiality, and suggests a GP elsewhere.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: does the assessment there and then, applies antibiotic stewardship, names z-drugs as controlled drugs with dependence risk, explores mood, alcohol and burnout without judgement, restricts record access, and keeps the working relationship warm.

avoid.dont: “Fine, just this once, but don’t tell anyone.”
avoid.instead: “I can’t prescribe without seeing you properly and recording it, but I can see you properly right now.”
avoid.why: Unrecorded prescribing without assessment breaches GMC prescribing guidance.

avoid.dont: “You’re a nurse, you should know better than to ask.”
avoid.instead: “I understand why it feels easier. Let me explain why I want to do it properly.”
avoid.why: Shaming her closes down the real problem and damages the working relationship.

avoid.dont: “We’ll just not write it on the system.”
avoid.instead: “Your record is confidential and we can restrict who can open it.”
avoid.why: Confidentiality is achieved by protecting records, not omitting them.

SCA_STEM.recent: Member of the practice nursing team. No booked appointment.
SCA_STEM.reason: Approaches the GP between patients: feels run down, not sleeping, thinks she has a chest infection; asks for antibiotics and ‘a few sleeping tablets’ without an appointment or a record.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] GMC Good medical practice (2024) · [2] GMC Good practice in proposing, prescribing, providing and managing medicines and devices (2021) · [3] GMC Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information (2017) · [4] NICE NG120 Cough (acute): antimicrobial prescribing (2019) · [5] NICE NG250 Pneumonia: diagnosis and management (2025) · [6] NICE TA77 Zaleplon, zolpidem and zopiclone for the short-term management of insomnia (2004) and NICE NG215 Medicines associated with dependence or withdrawal symptoms (2022) · [7] Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001: zopiclone and zolpidem, Schedule 4 Part 1
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A colleague asking for an unrecorded prescription is asking the GP to prescribe without an assessment and without a record, which GMC guidance does not allow for anyone [1, 2]. Working together is not in itself a bar to treating her, but the care must be a proper consultation, recorded like any other, with the same stewardship. Confidentiality is protected by access-controlled records, not by missing ones [3]. Antibiotics depend on assessment [4, 5]; hypnotics are short-term only and z-drugs are controlled drugs [6, 7]. The run-down, not-sleeping story deserves real attention, and she should be encouraged to have care from a GP outside her workplace.

points.t: Good medical practice [1]: wherever possible avoid providing medical care to yourself or anyone with whom you have a close personal relationship, and keep clear, accurate, contemporaneous records. The prescribing guidance [2] requires an adequate assessment and adequate knowledge of the patient’s health before prescribing, and a record of the prescription and the reasons. A colleague is not automatically a close personal relationship; what matters is objectivity, a proper assessment and a record.

Zopiclone and zolpidem are Schedule 4 Part 1 controlled drugs [7]. GMC [2]: controlled drugs must not be prescribed for yourself or someone close to you except in a genuine emergency when no one else can prescribe. For any patient, NICE TA77 [6] limits hypnotics to short-term use for severe insomnia; NG215 asks prescribers to discuss dependence and withdrawal before starting.

Assess properly: duration, fever, breathlessness, pleuritic pain, comorbidity, and observations including respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature and chest examination (booked in person on the record, not done informally). NICE NG120 [4]: most acute cough is self-limiting and does not need an antibiotic; a back-up prescription is an option for those at higher risk of complications. Suspected pneumonia is assessed with a severity score and treated per NICE NG250 [5].

She is owed the same confidentiality as any patient [3]. Colleagues should access her record only when involved in her care; practices can restrict access to staff records and audit access. Confidentiality means a protected record, not the absence of one.

Run down, not sleeping and wanting it hidden can signal stress, burnout, low mood, or reliance on hypnotics. Ask supportively about sleep, mood, alcohol, stress and work. Nurses have their own duty under the NMC Code (2018) to keep themselves fit to practise; occupational health can help if work is affected, with her consent.

Staff may be registered at their own practice, but a GP outside the workplace usually gives better privacy and objectivity, especially for mental health or ongoing problems. The practice should have a staff health policy; follow it.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Moves the conversation from the corridor to a private phone call; lets her say what she wants.
Workload, stress, relationships at work, fear of colleagues seeing her notes.
Picks up ‘not sleeping’, ‘run down’ and wanting no record as cues to a hidden agenda.
Idea (a quick script is easiest), concern (colleagues seeing her record), expectation (antibiotics and hypnotics, unrecorded).
Focused chest history; comorbidity, medicines, allergy; self-measured observations; in-person chest examination if any are abnormal.
Viral LRTI versus pneumonia; insomnia due to stress versus depression, alcohol or other causes.
Pneumonia red flags; mood and self-harm; self-sourcing or dependence on hypnotics.
Viral chest infection not needing antibiotics; stress-related insomnia.
Proper recorded consultation; no antibiotic per NG120; no hypnotic, with reasons; access-controlled record.
Encourages a GP outside the workplace; occupational health or workload support with consent.
Same-day contact if chest or mood worsens; review booked in two weeks; relationship preserved.

social.t: Healthcare staff often present late and informally. Heavy workload, shift patterns and stigma about mental health all make ‘corridor’ requests more likely.
Employees can self-certify for the first 7 calendar days of sickness; a fit note is needed after that. Fit notes can suggest workplace adjustments.

legal.t: Zopiclone and zolpidem are Schedule 4 Part 1 controlled drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001.
GMC Good medical practice (2024) requires clear, accurate, contemporaneous records. Accessing a colleague’s record without a care reason breaches confidentiality and data protection law.

professional.t: Prescribe only with adequate knowledge of the patient’s health; avoid prescribing for yourself or anyone close to you wherever possible; record what was prescribed and why.
The GP may be her colleague or employer. Keep clinical and employment roles separate; any concern about fitness to practise follows the practice policy and her own NMC Code (2018) duties.

community.t: Occupational health and any employee assistance programme; NHS Talking Therapies by self-referral; her own GP outside the practice.

redFlags: Breathlessness, pleuritic pain, high fever, abnormal observations: assess for pneumonia per NG250
Low mood with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm
Using hypnotics, alcohol or other substances to cope, or sourcing medicines informally
Impairment affecting safe practice at work
psychosocial: Fear of colleagues seeing her record
Embarrassment at being a patient where she works
ice: Idea: a quick unrecorded script is easiest
Concern: colleagues knowing her business, especially about sleep
Expectation: antibiotics and sleeping tablets without a record

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Your chest sounds like a viral infection that will settle without antibiotics, and the sleep problem sounds driven by stress rather than something a tablet will fix.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Sleeping tablets are like borrowing sleep on a credit card: they help for a night or two, but the bill comes with interest. Sorting out what’s keeping you awake pays it off.”

management.reflectIce: “Your worry is people here seeing your notes, so let’s protect your record rather than skip it.”
management.psychosocial: Treat her as a person under strain, not a rule-breaker; offer support at work only with her consent.
sharedPlan: No antibiotic: viral LRTI, per NG120; safety-net for pneumonia
No hypnotic: short-term only and controlled drug; sleep strategies
Register with a GP outside the practice; occupational health or Talking Therapies if wanted
safetyNet: Worsening chest, breathlessness or chest pain: same-day review
Low mood or self-harm thoughts: same-day contact; review in two weeks

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a professionalism station dressed as a favour. Marks go to holding the boundary warmly, turning the request into proper care, and finding the stressed person behind it.

items.fail: Writing the prescriptions to be helpful.
items.why: Prescribing without assessment or record breaches GMC guidance and risks harm.
items.fix: Offer a proper, recorded consultation instead.

items.fail: Giving antibiotics because she is a nurse and ‘knows’.
items.why: Stewardship applies to everyone; NG120 advises against antibiotics for most acute cough.
items.fix: Check observations properly, examine in person if needed, and decide on the findings.

items.fail: Prescribing a z-drug without exploring why she cannot sleep.
items.why: Z-drugs are controlled drugs with dependence risk; the cause is untreated.
items.fix: Explore stress, mood and alcohol; offer non-drug strategies.

items.fail: A curt refusal in the corridor.
items.why: She feels judged and will seek medicines elsewhere; the working relationship suffers.
items.fix: Take her somewhere private and explain the reasons kindly.

items.fail: Dismissing her worry about colleagues seeing her notes.
items.why: It is the real barrier to her getting care.
items.fix: Explain access controls and offer restriction; suggest a GP elsewhere.

items.why: An unrecorded encounter is unsafe for her and for you.
items.fix: Record the consultation, safety-net and book a review.
